findings.title: A slow HTTP body can inherit a replacement browser owner
findings.description: The public RPC route captures #browsers.get(clientId) after awaiting the body. A request started under socket A can finish after the same tab clientId was replaced by socket B; it then obtains B workerClientId and passes requireConnection. An old request therefore dispatches a new mutation under authority that did not exist when the request entered.
findings.reproduction: Actual production GatewayServer, Authentication, Ledger and Dispatcher with a local fake backend, partial HTTP body and real WebSocket replacement: originalOwner 2bf2a1ab-d37d-4b37-a923-45242858c001 became replacementOwner bc36fa1e-317b-40e2-98bf-94d5e6268c16; old turn/start forwarded under the replacement and ledger settled accepted. Evidence .work/v240/full2-owner-reproduction.json and .mjs.
findings.requestedFix: Capture the browser connection at HTTP admission before any awaited body read. Verify that exact captured connection at dispatch and final write; no connection becoming available later can grant the old request authority. Preserve accepted operation receipt replay. Add public HTTP slow-body replacement and missing-then-connected tests.
findings.coverageGap: Worker server tests cover event-channel revocation, but the public gateway rebind occurs before forwarding and is outside that test boundary.

findings.title: POSIX isolated-group stop signals a group after leader reaping
findings.description: In no-launcher POSIX isolatedGroup mode, stop retains the numeric child PID, signals -pid even if the child already exited, then waits for exitPromise and uses kill(-pid,0)/SIGKILL after the leader is reaped. If the old group is empty, that ID may be recycled for an unrelated group. This can falsely block cleanup or signal an unrelated same-user process group. Defaults/account probes use isolatedGroup in development and acceptance environments. The managed launcher branch is separately reviewed by the deployment reviewer.
findings.reproduction: Code-path proof from the actual close/stop implementation and ChildProcess exit/close lifecycle; no actual PID/PGID reuse was induced and no unrelated process was signaled.
findings.requestedFix: Bind group ownership to a live supervisor or other unambiguous process lifetime and retain responsibility for surviving descendants. Stop using the old numeric group after ownership can no longer be proved. Add regression for naturally exited leaders plus surviving descendants, without unsafe raw-PID cleanup.

findings.title: Windows Job fixture fallbacks can terminate a reused PID
findings.description: Several finally blocks first await owned Job/controller cleanup, then check alive(oldPid) and call process.kill(oldPid). At that point the intended child may already be dead and its PID reused. The fallback can terminate an unrelated process; the surrounding old-PID existence checks can also cause false reviewed-check failures. Actual controller/Job ownership is already available and should be the cleanup proof.
findings.reproduction: Read all fixture branches and controller contracts. No actual PID reuse or unrelated process kill was performed.
findings.requestedFix: Remove fallback termination by stale numeric PID. Use the owned ChildProcess/Job handle, exact creation identity or retained controller completion proof for cleanup. Preserve deliberate controller-death testing through its bound child handle. Update the same stale-PID liveness assertions listed in relatedFiles.
findings.relatedScope: Related files mostly perform signal-0 assertions only, not destructive fallback kills. Distinguish false-negative/false-positive cleanup evidence from the destructive windows-job fallbacks. Defaults lifecycle Windows creation-time check is stronger than POSIX PID-only fallback.

findings.title: Runtime resource policy conflates event and RPC frame budgets
findings.description: The README says responses/events retain full content within 12 MiB, but RuntimeService.emitEvent now enforces the shared 4 MiB event limit. Native wire/HTTP response frame limits remain 12 MiB and the private worker WebSocket buffered cap remains 16 MiB; those separate values are correct.
findings.requestedFix: Document the distinct event, RPC frame and buffered-output limits and recovery behavior without changing the valid 12 MiB native frame or 16 MiB private backlog values.

method: Independent semantic source and test review on the frozen snapshot. All 106 associated test/fixture/README files were content-read in this round, including native integration bodies, cleanup ordering, fixture isolation and actual assertions; no inventory-only test is counted. Core/gateway/shared and central runtime ownership, lifecycle, history, conversion, attachments, service dispatch, worker HTTP, validation and witness modules were reread end-to-end. The 35 other runtime modules listed under priorFullReadRevalidated were fully read in round1; their current caller/consumer contracts and tests were revalidated against the current service, validation and protocol boundaries. Their recorded modification times precede round1 freeze, but timestamps are corroborating observations rather than cryptographic old-content proof. The four round1 repairs were rechecked in source and regression assertions. An isolated actual public GatewayServer slow-body reproduction confirmed the owner-transfer finding. No full test suite, paid model inference, production access or external MCP request was performed. Protocol generated content regeneration is owned independently by the parent; here ModelList provider selection, ProcessExited outputDrainTimedOut, GatewayOAuth prompt, ordinary fork independence and resume excludeTurns consumers were checked against selected generated schema properties, without claiming full generated-schema byte review.
